title: Ahead in material, still unable to win
outcomes: Explains why an extra pawn does not win in the opposite-bishop family shown
Names the square the defending king must keep covering
Tells a held fortress from a broken one, and a position with nothing to defend

steps.text:
A **fortress** is a set-up the stronger side cannot break, even when it is ahead. Here both sides have a bishop, on opposite colours, and White has one extra pawn, yet White cannot win.
In these examples the defender has a king beside the square the pawn needs next and a bishop with safe waiting moves. The tablebase confirms each example; it does not prove the same holds for other pawns or bishop colours.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has the extra pawn, on b6, with a bishop behind it on a7.

line.say: Black waits with the bishop. The king stays where it covers b7.
White's king walks toward the pawn.
Black waits again with the bishop.

claims.statement: The tablebase shows the position is a draw.
The king on c8 covers b7.
White has the only pawn on the board.

steps.text:
**When it holds.** In these examples the draw holds while the black king stays next to the square in front of the pawn (or on it) and the bishop has waiting moves; moving the king two files away from the pawn's file, as in Kd7 or Kd8, loses by the tablebase.
**Rule of thumb:** Before you trust a fortress, name the square the extra pawn needs and which of your pieces guards it; then check with a tablebase or engine rather than assuming.

steps.title: Same pieces, one change
steps.prompt: White to move in each position. Can White win? Predict, then check.
Which part was hardest: seeing which square the pawn needs, seeing that only the king can guard it, or accepting that being ahead did not win?
